title: A filename can display with a totally different extension than the one splitext actually finds
assumption: The characters your eyes read, left to right, are the characters the code is operating on.

input.description: A malicious email attachment or download name designed to visually read as a harmless document while actually being an executable.

what_goes_wrong: A person reviewing the filename in a file list or email client sees what renders as "invoiceexe.doc" (the override reverses everything after it) and approves it as a document, while the real file, in logical order, is "invoice" + override + "cod.exe" — a .exe file.
why: U+202E is a Unicode bidirectional-formatting control character that tells a rendering engine to display everything after it in right-to-left visual order, with no change at all to the underlying code point sequence. splitext/extname operate on that unchanged logical sequence, so they correctly report the real extension as ".exe"; it is only the ON-SCREEN rendering a human uses to judge the file that gets visually reversed into something else entirely.
affects: any renderer following the unicode bidirectional algorithm (terminals, file managers, email clients)
python os.path.splitext (reports the true, unreversed extension)
node path.extname (reports the true, unreversed extension)

repros.code:
import os.path
RLO = "\u202e"
name = "invoice" + RLO + "cod.exe"
print([hex(ord(c)) for c in name])
print("real extension:", os.path.splitext(name)[1])

fix: Reject or strip Unicode bidirectional control characters (U+202A-U+202E, U+2066-U+2069) from filenames before display or validation, and always trust the logical extension splitext/extname reports, never what a filename visually appears to end in.

sources.title: Unicode Technical Report #9: Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm

test_cases.note: Your extension check should see '.exe' here even though the filename could render on screen as something else entirely.
